page.title: Day 7 against Neave's manual
page.standfirst_html: Every flag the comparator raised for Day 7, adjudicated against J.Day.7.14Feb22.pdf — the extracted text for wording, and twelve page images for numbers, emphasis and the two things pdftotext cannot read at all on this day: a binder-tab cover letter and a whole page set in a cipher font. The biggest single finding is not a word swap: the Major Activity's introduction has been substantially reworded, and two of its source paragraphs never made it into the QMD at all. Decide each one; export the file; I make the edits and open the PR.

sections.title: Fix proposed
sections.note_html: Each one is a word-for-word difference from the source that I judge a transcription defect. Blue underline is what Neave wrote; struck red is what the site says instead. D7-11 is the one to read first: it is not a wording slip but a substantially rewritten paragraph that changes what Deming is claimed to have thought.

items.source_html: ...primarily interested in <mark class='src'>idling</mark> away their time...
items.site_html: ...primarily interested in <mark class='gone'>sitting</mark> away their time...
items.proposal: ...primarily interested in idling away their time and getting away with the absolute minimum possible effort...
items.evidence_html: Confirmed on the page image, printed p1: Neave writes "idling away their time", describing workers he believes are wrongly assumed to be lazy. "Sitting away" isn't idiomatic English and inverts the sense of the sentence's own next clause ("getting away with the absolute minimum possible effort").

items.source_html: ...the £197,000 cost of the <mark class='src'>fake</mark> calls.
items.site_html: ...the £197,000 cost of the <mark class='gone'>false</mark> calls.
items.proposal: The company has also paid £1,021,000 in service payments, the £122,000 cost of investigating the fraud, and the £197,000 cost of the fake calls."
items.evidence_html: Confirmed on the page image, printed p15. Neave's own italicised aside two lines below reinforces the word: "[Apparently about 1.25 million bogus calls had been made!]" — bogus and fake are the same claim; "false calls" reads as a different, blander one (calls that didn't connect, rather than calls that were staged).

items.source_html: I had gone up to the office to submit my report as usual (<mark class='src'>religious</mark>), but the lady was not there.
items.site_html: I had gone up to the office to submit my report as usual (<mark class='gone'>religiously</mark>), but the lady was not there.
items.proposal: I had gone up to the office to submit my report as usual (religious), but the lady was not there.
items.evidence_html: The page image confirms Neave's PDF really does print "(religious)", not "(religiously)" — almost certainly his own slip, since the storyteller uses the correct adverb two sentences earlier ("I religiously submitted this report"). The site silently corrected it at some point with no entry in docs/deviations/. Two ways to close this: revert to the literal (if odd) source wording, or keep the correction and log it retroactively as a sanctioned typo fix. Your call — I don't have a strong preference between them.
items.decision_note: Keep the correction and log it retroactively as a sanctioned typo fix. Should we also add [sic] here in the text?
items.outcome: Kept the corrected 'religiously'; logged retroactively in docs/deviations/2026-09-01-day-7-religious-typo-sanctioned.md. No [sic] added — see that entry for why.

items.proposal:
So, finally, on to Deming's "parade of obstacles": there are no less than 16 of them. Although you are now already very familiar with the 13th of these (regarding conformance to specifications), the topics are mostly ones that have not been mentioned previously. The Obstacles are generally more tightly focused than the issues in the 14 Points and the Deadly Diseases, and so it may well be quicker and easier for you to "get your teeth into" some of them: they should usually not demand as much breadth and depth of thought as often needed with those larger issues. Be relaxed about timings this afternoon: feel free to concentrate on the ones that strike you as being of greatest interest.

Some of the Obstacles are versed in terms most relevant to manufacturing. However, as we have seen previously, there are likely to be analogies with other areas that could be worth investigating: what Deming writes in such terms is often found to be just as relevant elsewhere if expressed slightly differently. But, remembering when Out of the Crisis was written (the mid-1980s), I rather suspect that Dr Deming was particularly keen to help manufacturing companies in America, realising the danger that, unless they changed, much of their business would soon be lost to companies on the other side of the world. Sadly, I fear that many did not listen.

So, even if you are not involved in manufacturing, devote some thought as to whether such analogies may exist in your own line of business. For example, Deming often uses the term "production workers", but obviously that can be generally interpreted simply as those who do the work compared with those whose job is to manage it. However if, after some thought, you feel sure that a particular Obstacle cannot be relevant in your area of activity then feel free to move on and spend extra time on those that are.

For years, in my seminar "Understanding the Deming Philosophy", I asked delegates to recount stories from their own experience which illustrated why Dr Deming regarded all that follow as being "Obstacles" to the progress he wanted us to make. Invariably those stories came so thick and fast that I would be surprised if you do not also quickly think of some while being introduced to the Obstacles. While they are fresh in mind, write down brief accounts in the spaces provided. Also try to expand on the problems that these Obstacles pose and then consider the situation in "your organisation" (interpreted if necessary as on Day 6 page 3). Does some form of that Obstacle exist there and, if so, what might be done about it?

Since my coverage of most of these Obstacles in DemDim is very brief, I'll expand a little more on them in the following pages. In each case, read both my sentence or two in DemDim (pages 52–55) followed by my comments on the coming pages. It isn't necessary for me to provide any more than this since Dr Deming's discussions of the Obstacles in Out of the Crisis are particularly clear and helpful. However, if you do not have a copy of Out of the Crisis then I would therefore be putting you at something of a disadvantage! So, just in case, I have reproduced some extracts from the Out of the Crisis coverage on Appendix pages 32–37. (In many cases there is, of course, much more in Out of the Crisis.) In what follows, I have referenced the relevant page(s) in both the Appendix and Out of the Crisis.

[NB callout] As indicated at the bottom of DemDim page 10, I think there can be no doubt that, like me, Dr Deming regretted the weakness of the English language in lacking single words for "he or she", "him or her", "man or woman", etc. In the circumstances, and as you will have seen before, Dr Deming makes no bones about referring to people, both male and female, simply in the masculine form. Of course, he did not intend any offence by so doing, and indeed traditionally his use of English is correct. I repeat this here because, within the extracts I have chosen, such usage appears quite often, and again I beg that this may cause no offence. In the rare cases that he uses the feminine form, it is usually because he is thinking of a particular individual.
items.evidence_html:
This is the pass's one big finding, and it's several defects at once, all in the same run of text on printed p27:
  1. Two whole source paragraphs are missing from the QMD, not paraphrased: the "production workers" analogy paragraph (Missing Gap 2–3) and the "Understanding the Deming Philosophy" seminar-stories paragraph (Missing Gap 4). Both read clean on the page image; neither is page furniture.
  2. The opening paragraph's supporting sentences were replaced with a four-item bulleted list not in the source ("referred to on Days 4 and 5...main topic of the previous few pages...") — invented framing, not a rewording of anything on the page.
  3. A specific claim was substituted for a different one. The source says Deming (writing in the mid-1980s) was concerned that American manufacturing companies would lose business to overseas competition if they didn't change. The site instead has Neave saying some Obstacles have "become considerably worse—particularly in the field of education" — a different, unsupported claim the page image does not contain anywhere (confirmed: this sentence scored 23% against the entire Day 7 PDF corpus, i.e. it resembles nothing in it — Unsourced 9).
  4. The gendered-language NB callout cites the wrong source. The page image shows Neave's footnote is to DemDim page 10. The site's NB cites "Appendix page 31" instead — not just a wrong number but the wrong book, which is the most consequential class of defect this site can carry (#738).
This clearly predates docs/deviations/ (no entry exists) and is too large for a one-line fix — the proposal restores the source's five-paragraph structure and wording in full, including the two missing paragraphs and the correct DemDim citation. I've kept the existing markdown link enrichments (Appendix/Day-6 cross-references) where the source itself makes the same point, since removing working navigation isn't the goal here — only the invented content and the wrong citation are. Please read this one in full before deciding; it's the one place in this pass where I'd genuinely value your read over mine.
items.decision_note: “parade of obstacles” and “production workers” are Deming quotes - should be in blue, as per the convention. All your other suggestions look good.
items.outcome: Applied in full, with 'parade of obstacles' and 'production workers' wrapped in .deming_quote per Lee's note. 'Day 6 page 3' left as plain text (no #sec-page3 anchor exists in content/days/day-06/ to link to).

sections.note_html: pdftotext discards every italic and bold, so no automated flag in this epic can see any of these — all three came from reading the source pages directly, while looking at the pages above for other reasons.

items.source_html: ...the majority who are at the receiving end of these approaches...they are those who are—or, sadly, in some cases, were (past tense)—wholly committed to their work...
items.site_html: ...both set in roman on the site.
items.proposal: ...the majority who are at the *receiving* end of these approaches... ...they are those who are—or, sadly, in some cases, *were* (past tense)—wholly committed to their work...
items.evidence_html: Both italics carry real contrasts in Neave's argument: receiving (as opposed to applying) these management techniques, and were (as opposed to are) wholly committed — the past tense doing the work of saying some good people gave up. Set in roman, the second reads as a stray parenthetical instead of the sentence's actual point.

items.evidence_html: The Finance Director's dawning realisation turns on this word — the system meets the target, but only by luck, not by being capable of it. Confirmed on the page image, printed p12.
